summary: This benchmark evaluates a confidence-gated routing mechanism between a 7B specialist (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) and a 14B model graft across 2,304 matched Python repair triplets. The methodology is rigorous and preregistered, demonstrating statistically significant gains against decoy bracket distractions while bounding neutral regression within pre-set tolerances. While the benchmark domain is synthetic, the experimental discipline, paired controls, and mathematical consistency are commendable.
strengths: Rigorous statistical controls including paired differences, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, and budget-matched random baselines across 32 seeds.
Flawless internal mathematical consistency between raw prompt counts, group outcomes, and reported percentages.
Explicit pre-registration and confirmation structure with frozen thresholds and disjoint test IDs avoiding data contamination.
Exemplary hardware, software environment, and model revision pinning down to exact commit hashes and peak memory allocations.
weaknesses: The evaluation task is narrow and synthetic (delimiter repair with decoy brackets vs. letters), which limits generalizability to real-world code generation or refactoring tasks.
Practical deployment performance such as end-to-end inference latency and memory throughput is not benchmarked across the full panel.
The exposition is exceptionally dense and telegraphic, requiring readers to cross-reference multiple prior study READMEs for full architectural context.
suggestions: Extend the confidence routing benchmark to standard open coding benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MultiPL-E, or SWE-bench Lite) to validate broader applicability.
Include end-to-end wall-clock latency and memory throughput measurements comparing standalone inference, full routing overhead, and always-blended passes on standard serving runtimes.
